claims.text: Increasing sugar-sweetened soft drink consumption from 1 or fewer drinks per week to 1 or more drinks per day is associated with greater weight gain over a 4-year period in women.
Decreasing sugar-sweetened soft drink consumption is associated with smaller weight gain over a 4-year period in women.
Increased consumption of fruit punch is associated with greater weight gain compared with decreased consumption in women.
Consuming 1 or more sugar-sweetened soft drinks per day is associated with an increased relative risk of type 2 diabetes compared with consuming less than 1 per month.
Consuming 1 or more fruit punch drinks per day is associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes compared with consuming less than 1 per month.

evidence.description: Multivariate-adjusted mean weight gain was 4.69 kg for 1991 to 1995 and 4.20 kg for 1995 to 1999 among women increasing soft drink intake from <=1/week to >=1/day.
Multivariate-adjusted mean weight gain was 1.34 kg for 1991 to 1995 and 0.15 kg for 1995 to 1999 among women who decreased soft drink intake.
Increased consumption of fruit punch was associated with greater weight gain compared with decreased consumption after adjusting for lifestyle and dietary confounders.
Women consuming >=1 sugar-sweetened soft drink per day had a relative risk of type 2 diabetes of 1.83 (95% CI, 1.42-2.36; P<.001 for trend) compared with <1 drink per month.
Fruit punch consumption >=1 drink per day compared with <1 drink per month had an RR of 2.00 (95% CI, 1.33-3.03; P=.001) for type 2 diabetes.

methodologies.name: Prospective Cohort Study
methodologies.description: Prospective cohort analysis tracking dietary intake, body weight changes, and incident type 2 diabetes over eight years of follow-up.
conditions: Women free of diabetes and major chronic diseases at baseline in 1991
Dietary information and weight ascertained in 1991, 1995, and 1999

limitations.text: Relationships between sugar-sweetened beverage consumption, weight gain, and type 2 diabetes risk had been minimally addressed in adults prior to this study.
